details:
**Daniel in the lions' den**
The book's most famous story and the usual giveaway. After King Darius the Mede is tricked into signing a decree forbidding prayer to anyone but himself for thirty days, Daniel keeps praying to God and is thrown into a den of lions. God sends an angel to shut the lions' mouths, and Daniel survives the night unharmed.

**Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego in the fiery furnace**
Daniel's three companions refuse to bow to a golden statue, sixty cubits high and six cubits wide, set up by King Nebuchadnezzar II of Babylon. They are thrown into a fiery furnace but emerge unharmed, and a fourth figure "like a son of the gods" is seen walking with them in the flames.

**Belshazzar's feast and the writing on the wall**
At a feast held by the Babylonian ruler Belshazzar, a disembodied hand writes "Mene, mene, tekel, upharsin" on the palace wall; the source of the phrase "the writing on the wall." Daniel interprets it as a sign that the kingdom has been weighed and found wanting and will be divided, and Belshazzar is slain that night as Darius the Mede takes the kingdom. Belshazzar had promised whoever read it purple clothing, a gold chain, and the rank of third ruler in the kingdom.

**Nebuchadnezzar's dream of the statue with feet of clay**
Nebuchadnezzar dreams of a great statue with a head of gold, chest of silver, belly of bronze, legs of iron, and feet of iron mixed with clay. A stone cut without hands strikes the feet, destroys the statue, and grows into a mountain; Daniel interprets the metals as successive kingdoms to be replaced by God's eternal kingdom. This is the origin of the phrase "feet of clay."

**The ram and the goat**
In Daniel 8, Daniel sees a two-horned ram destroyed by a goat with a single great horn. The goat's horn breaks and is replaced by four horns; the angel Gabriel explains that the ram represents Media and Persia and the goat represents Greece, whose kingdom splits into four. Daniel is told that afterward "the sanctuary will be cleansed."

**Susanna and Bel and the Dragon**
Deuterocanonical additions found in the Greek version of Daniel and in Catholic and Orthodox Bibles. In Susanna, two lecherous elders who spied on her bathing falsely accuse her of adultery and are exposed and executed when Daniel questions them separately. In Bel and the Dragon, Daniel proves that priests, not the idol Bel, are secretly eating the offerings, and he kills a dragon worshipped by the Babylonians.

**Refusing the king's food**
At the start of the book, Daniel and his companions (whose Hebrew names are Hananiah, Mishael, and Azariah) refuse the king's meat and wine and eat only pulse (vegetables) and water for ten days. They end up healthier, "fairer and fatter," than the others and are found ten times better than all the king's magicians and enchanters.

**Vision of the four beasts and "one like a son of man"**
In Daniel 7, Daniel sees four beasts rising from the sea, representing four kingdoms. He then sees God as the "Ancient of Days" on a throne, and "one like a son of man" coming with the clouds of heaven receives an everlasting dominion over the world.

**Nebuchadnezzar's tree dream and madness**
Nebuchadnezzar dreams of a great, fruitful tree that shelters all animals and from which "all flesh was fed," until it is cut down. Daniel explains that the tree is the king himself, who is then driven out to live like a beast for seven years, eating grass like an ox, until he acknowledges God.

**Belteshazzar**
The Babylonian name given to Daniel by Nebuchadnezzar, who made him "chief of the magicians" for his skill at interpreting dreams. Daniel serves several kings of Babylon and Persia over the course of the book.

**The Archangel Michael and the prince of Persia**
In Daniel 10, a heavenly man with a body like beryl and a face like lightning appears to Daniel and explains that he was delayed fighting the "prince of Persia" until Michael came to help him. The book's final chapters also describe wars between the "king of the north" and the "king of the south."

**"Time, times, and half a time"**
A prophetic period mentioned in Daniel 7 and 12, interpreted as three and a half years. It is often linked with the 1,260 days of Revelation in apocalyptic interpretations of biblical prophecy.

**Seventy weeks prophecy**
In Daniel 9, Daniel reflects on Jeremiah's prediction that Jerusalem's desolation would last seventy years. The angel Gabriel reinterprets it as seventy "weeks" of years.

**Composition under Antiochus IV**
Most modern scholars date the book's final form to the 2nd century BCE, during the persecution of Jews by the Seleucid king Antiochus IV Epiphanes, although it is set during the Babylonian Exile. Parts of the book are written in Aramaic rather than Hebrew.
